Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago.
  • NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," noted Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia.
  • Industry observers note that for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago. To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set new financial records as demand for its AI accelerators reveals no signs of slowing down. The company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion.

"Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," noted Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.".

Industry observers note that for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The company's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago.

Industry observers note that as expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the tech giant's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year.

Industry observers note that one of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The firm also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform.

Industry observers note that "Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress said. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028.".

Industry observers note that to support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The organization's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The company expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though given the fact that its purchases in FY2028 are set to exceed $200 billion, expect its procurements in FY2030 to be higher.

The commitments reflect Nvidia's efforts to ensure that its suppliers can manufacture sufficient quantities of advanced processors, memory, substrates, and packaging components. In addition to its existing agreements with partners like TSMC, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, Nvidia on Wednesday declared fresh partnerships with Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Kinsus for substrates, as well as SPIL for advanced packaging. In addition, the company disclosed agreements with Amkor, Ibiden, KYEC, and Unimicron.

Industry observers note that during the earnings call, Kress stated that demand for Nvidia's products continues to exceed available supply, prompting the tech giant to work with manufacturing partners to expand production capacity. She also indicated that Nvidia could provide suppliers with prepayments or other financial assistance to accelerate capacity expansion.

Recent findings suggest that although these procurement commitments are gargantuan, Nvidia expects demand for its AI infrastructure to remain strong, which will justify the expenditures. The firm raised its revenue growth forecast for FY2028 from approximately 70% to 75% due to stronger demand and additional manufacturing capacity that it expects to secure.

In addition to its supply commitments, Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in agreements with neocloud providers that allow it to earn revenue from hardware sales and participate in cloud rental revenue above a guaranteed minimum. Meanwhile, the organization's maximum financial exposure under various guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike AI data center campus in Ohio, which will serve OpenAI under 20-year leases.

In total, Nvidia's commitments reached $540 billion as of early Q4 FY2024.

Nvidia currently absorbs higher component and manufacturing costs to honor existing purchase orders and maintain previously agreed prices for its customers. As a result, the tech giant expects its GAAP gross margin to decline from 74.8% in Q3 FY2027 to 71% – 72% in Q4, which it considers the bottom of the current margin cycle.

Going forward, Nvidia plans to introduce revised pricing in FY2028 to help offset higher supply costs and restore profitability, which is when the company expects gross margins to recover to 72% – 73% next fiscal year, although it has not disclosed the magnitude of its planned price adjustments or the products they will affect.

"We thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that, and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included," Kress remarked. "What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that was held solid as we moved to a newly introduced pricing, as we moved into the new year.".

Perhaps more importantly is that Colette Kress largely sidestepped the question about custom AI accelerators and their potential impact on Nvidia's pricing power. During the conference call, an analyst asked whether Nvidia would accept lower margins to protect its market share against custom AI accelerators developed by hyperscalers. The interim CEO avoided directly addressing whether competition from custom silicon could undermine Nvidia’s competitive position, leaving considerable room for speculation.

For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion ±3%, which would represent an increase of about 12% sequentially. The organization expects GAAP gross margin of 71% to 72% and GAAP operating expenses of approximately $11 billion during the quarter. Nvidia’s forecast excludes Data Center compute revenue from China and accounts for an additional week in the quarter. While Nvidia expects its gross margin to decline during the Vera Rubin transition, Kress mentioned that the company anticipates a recovery to 72% – 73% in FY2028.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Since President Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, Elon Musk has been one of his biggest allies in Silicon Valley.
  • But in an interview at this week’s annual DealBook Summit, Musk suddenly sang a different tune.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since President Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, Elon Musk has been one of his biggest allies in Silicon Valley. The Tesla CEO has served as both Trump’s employee and his friend: He spearheaded the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency, aka DOGE, and wasn’t shy to tell the press that he came to “love” Trump over the course of their work together. But in an interview at this week’s annual DealBook Summit, Musk suddenly sang a different tune. “I’m not MAGA,” Musk remarked. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” Musk may claim not to know the full extent of what “MAGA” means, but in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, he was happy to embrace the term. Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

Industry observers note that there's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Recent findings suggest that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

Recent findings suggest that the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint indicates so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

Industry observers note that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Industry observers note that use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

In a recent development, every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Sources indicate that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

It has been revealed that don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF highlights what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

In a recent development, retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Sources indicate that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

It has been revealed that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Army is planning to blow up roughly 5 tons of bomb-making materials in Iowa on Friday, a volatile event expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air as far as 90 miles away.
  • Recent findings suggest that the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, the unusual event may sound like a side quest straight out of Grand Theft Auto VI, but it holds potentially serious health consequences for people in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Army is planning to blow up roughly 5 tons of bomb-making materials in Iowa on Friday, a volatile event expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air as far as 90 miles away. The chemicals are unstable enough that moving them poses a high risk of explosion, a fact that makes a planned detonation the comparatively safe option. The unusual event may sound like a side quest straight out of Grand Theft Auto VI, but it holds potentially serious health consequences for people in the area. The detonation is set to take place at noon Central time at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in the southeast corner of the state. The Army described the planned explosion’s hazards in an advisory to local residents, noting that the long-stored barrels of unstable lead azide are expected to create elevated levels of airborne lead when detonated. The advisory states that lead levels are expected to remain below the threshold “at which EPA would require protective actions be taken,” but goes on to describe many measures that residents should take to protect themselves during the event. “The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” it continues. “Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and see a plume of dust which is expected to linger for no more than one hour after the detonation, depending on wind speed.” The explosion is expected to be large enough that locals close to Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park could experience “localized window damage.” Residents have been asked to leave their houses for six hours on the day of the detonation, as both locations are less than a quarter of a mile from the detonation zone. 2 lead exposure pathways pose serious dangers The Army is also cautioning people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors, keep windows closed, and set their heating and cooling units to recirculate air within their homes in order to minimize potential exposure. Schools in communities including Danville and Mediapolis will close Friday to protect students from lead exposure—both airborne dust and settled dust. “Deposition of lead-containing dust may occur after the detonation on surfaces within certain areas affected by the detonation plume,” the Army’s warning states, encouraging residents to wet-clean surfaces exposed to the chemical dust after the explosion takes place. The advisory, which also includes a map predicting the path of the toxic dust, warns that children, pregnant women, and older adults in particular should avoid contact with lead particles. Only about 400 people live in the Iowa town where the blast will take place, but toxic dust is expected to drift into the air and deposit itself 30 miles north in more populated neighboring communities like Morning Sun, Mediapolis, and Wapello. Airborne lead dust could cause problems to people who inhale it as far away as Cedar Rapids, which is 90 miles from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Even Illinois, the state next door, is on high alert for the explosion. “There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks,” Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a health advisory. “Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pixel Tag will begin selling in Europe soon, according to a recent leak. The Android Find Hub tracker sold nearly everywhere else during the initial launch.

Google’s very first tracker joined the dozens of other options that work on the Android Find Hub network, launching alongside the Pixel 11 earlier in the year. It’s a sleek little tracking tag, with some first-party care that makes it stand out.

Sources indicate that leaker Roland Quandt posted an update on the Pixel Tag in a recent Bluesky post. It states the Pixel Tag will, in fact, be sold in Europe. There’s no timeline indication in the post, other than a wide-open “pretty soon” tagged on at the end.

According to recent reports, it’s a wonder it didn’t launch in Europe to begin with. Google initially listed 8 countries, including the US, Canada, Australia, India, and Japan. The United Kingdom is included in that list, but the larger portion classified as the European Union is left out.

The leak also eases a major concern for customers – whether the Pixel Tag will be operational in Europe at all. The Pixel Tag would likely function among the network of Android users in the varying regions, but there’s no definitive answer. Even though Nvidia states that it does not blueprint to bring its former CEO Jensen Huang back to the firm, that hasn't stopped some of its board members from continuing to lobby for his return. Following the news that some of Huang's allies have formed a "war room" to drive his reinstatement just days after his resignation, one Nvidia employee went so far as to warn that the company faces the possibility of an exodus of "irreplaceable talent" if Huang isn't reinstated. We've even seen U.S. President Trump argue for giving Huang his old job back, but the company said during its November 17 earnings call that wasn't in the cards. Now, Semafor reports that some Nvidia board members aren't taking "no" for an answer.

It has been revealed that huang, for his part, has already stated that he would be "honored" to return to the organization that he resigned from in disgrace just a few days ago. At the time, he admitted to having an affair with a woman who worked for Megaspeed, a controversial Nvidia customer linked to the smuggling of export-controlled AI hardware into China. That woman has also been accused of being a Chinese spy, further complicating an already troublesome matter for Nvidia and Huang. Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer will make an appearance before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees in early December and are likely to face some difficult questions.

Industry observers note that but despite all of this, Huang is mentioned to have spoken with at least one Nvidia board member about the possibility of making a return to Nvidia. That meeting took place hours before Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the manufacturer’s earnings call that Huang wasn't coming back. The board voted unanimously to accept his resignation, and won't be backtracking. It's reported that three board members don't agree with that stance, while others have already turned their attention to who will replace Huang long-term. Interim CEO Colette Kress is not being considered as a full-time replacement for Huang.

According to recent reports, instead, Arm CEO Rene Haas has appeared as a frontrunner for the top job, with the Nvidia board believed to have already made an approach. Marvell CEO Matt Murphy is also another name under consideration, but the ongoing calls for Huang to be brought back into the fold are thought to have put him off. Rene Haas has reportedly been considere.

It isn't just some of Nvidia's board members who have rallied around Huang. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney have also chimed in, while a Taiwanese skyscraper was used to send messages of support to a man who has proven hugely popular in the country.

#11496. Young people may be holding back gender equality at work

Young people may be holding back gender equality at work

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About two decades ago, a substantial body of academic research started to provide evidence for what many had long suspected: Young people were leading the way toward a more gender-equal world.
  • About two decades ago, a substantial body of academic research started to provide evidence for what many had long suspected: Young people were leading the way toward a more gender-equal world.
  • Sources indicate that european Social Survey data from 2004 and 2010 found that younger adults were considerably less likely than their older counterparts to endorse traditional gender roles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About two decades ago, a substantial body of academic research started to provide evidence for what many had long suspected: Young people were leading the way toward a more gender-equal world. European Social Survey data from 2004 and 2010 found that younger adults were considerably less likely than their older counterparts to endorse traditional gender roles. In 2009, Pew Research found that Americans under the age of 30 were considerably more liberal in their attitudes toward women’s roles than older generations. And in 2015, a study published in Psychology of Women Quarterly found that millennials held more egalitarian attitudes toward women’s work and family roles than baby boomers had at the same age. The direction of travel seemed clear: Each upcoming generation was broadly more supportive of gender equality than the last. Over the last few years, though, there’s been a disconcerting shift. In several recent surveys, young men—and in some cases young women—have expressed more traditional attitudes toward gender roles, and greater skepticism about efforts to advance women’s equality, than men old enough to be their fathers or grandfathers. And there’s evidence that this generational divide extends to attitudes toward leadership, too. This month, the Reykjavík Index for Leadership—an annual study conducted by global research firm Verian and the Reykjavík Global Foundation, an Iceland-based nonprofit—found that younger adults are considerably less likely than their older counterparts to believe women and men are equally suited to lead. “The assumptions around sociodemographics and values and attitudes that we were able to make until the 2020s no longer hold in the same way,” says Michelle Harrison, global president at Verian Group and cofounder of the index. “We understand we are in a new geopolitical and technological paradigm.” The findings raise troubling questions for businesses that have spent decades working to advance gender equality: What happens when the next generation of leaders appears less convinced of its importance than the last? And what can organizations do to change people’s minds? A growing generational divide Launched in 2018, the Reykjavík Index measures perceptions of gender-equal leadership across 23 sectors, from politics to technology. Its latest survey questioned more than 11,000 adults across the G7—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States—and four other countries, asking whether men, women, or both are equally suited to lead. A score of 100 represents universal agreement that men and women are equally suited to leadership. After reaching a peak of 73 in 2019, the G7’s overall index score has steadily declined. This year, it edged up for the first time in seven years, rising one point to 69. But the modest recovery masks a real generational divide. Across the G7, 18- to 34-year-olds recorded an index score of just 65, compared with 74 among 55- to 65-year-olds. The gap itself is not new—it has existed since the index was launched in 2018—but it has tripled from three to nine points in that time, and the youngest group’s score has also fallen five points over the same period. The divide is particularly stark in Britain and France, where younger adults trail their older counterparts by 14 points. And while young men’s attitudes have shown signs of improvement in several countries over the past year, the broader picture remains troubling. Younger adults are still the least likely to view men and women as equally suited to lead. These findings corroborate other studies. In 2025, a 30-country study by Ipsos and King’s College London found that Gen Z men and women were more divided on questions of feminism, gender roles, and women’s rights than any other generation surveyed. Some 57% of Gen Z men agreed that efforts to promote women’s equality had gone so far that they discriminated against men, compared with 36% of Gen Z women and 44% of boomer men. The power of the manosphere Experts offer different explanations for what has caused the generational shift in attitudes. Many, however, mention social media’s ability to shape cultural scripts. “Contemporary online communities such as the manosphere are vocally opposed to women behaving in agentic or assertive ways. This includes in the home and in the workplace,” says Rachael Robnett, a professor of psychology and director of the Women’s Research Institute of Nevada at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. “To the extent that young men are disproportionately engaged in the manosphere relative to other generations, it makes sense that they would show less positive attitudes about women’s leadership ability,” she adds. Jess Carbino, a sociologist and author, agrees. “I believe the generational divide may reflect cyclical changes happening in how feminism and gender roles are being signaled in the media, particularly on social media,” she says. Another possibility, Carbino suggests, is that we’re witnessing a backlash against changing economic and social norms. The share of women who earn as much as—or significantly more than—their husbands has approximately tripled over the past 50 years, according to Pew Research data. For a brief period earlier this year, there were more women in non-farm payroll jobs in the U.S. than men, according to federal data. These changes have challenged long-standing assumptions about men as breadwinners and women as caregivers, and for some men, Carbino suggests, that shift can feel threatening. “When masculinity feels threatened—by earning less than a partner, for example, or by losing status at work—some men withdraw from domains culturally coded as feminine, like caregiving and housework,” she explains. Such responses can reinforce the very stereotypes that gender-equality initiatives have sought to dismantle: assumptions about who should lead a manufacturer, who should earn the family income, and who should stay home to raise children. Related to this, Kent Bausman, a professor of sociology at Maryville University of Saint Louis, says that economic pressure and economic insecurity can “breed a sense of zero-sum gain in the competition for jobs and resources.” Young men who are “still socialized as the traditional economic provider interpret women’s expansion in opportunities across various walks of life as a threat to their own economic prospects,” he adds. A workplace opportunity For Harrison, the latest findings present employers with both a challenge and an opportunity. While the generational divide threatens to complicate efforts to advance gender equality, workplaces may also be among the most important settings in which attitudes can change. Unlike the online spaces where young people may encounter rigid ideas about masculinity and femininity, workplaces can expose them to different models of leadership, collaboration, and authority. Seeing women succeed in senior positions and men thrive in roles traditionally associated with women helps to challenge assumptions about who is suited to lead. Carbino argues that employers can make those examples more visible, creating opportunities for employees to learn from leaders who defy traditional expectations. “Employers can elevate and highlight women’s leadership,” she says. “They can engage in programs in which women mentor both men and women.” Ultimately, Carbino remains hopeful that the “pendulum will swing back.” Historically, she notes, periods of backlash against feminism have often been followed by renewed progress. Robnett, too, cautions against interpreting the findings as evidence that an entire generation has rejected gender equality. Although some young men hold more traditional attitudes than their older counterparts, not all of them do. “Although we need to continue to push for change in these negative attitudes, it is encouraging that most young men perceive women and men as equally suited to leadership roles,” she says. Indeed, there are tentative signs of progress: The G7’s overall index score has begun to recover, and young men’s scores have risen in five of the seven countries surveyed. Whether that recovery lasts remains uncertain, Harrison says. But, she adds, the findings suggest that the next generation’s attitudes toward gender equality are not set in stone—and that the workplaces they enter could help shape what comes next.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

College may cost much less than you think, according to this calculator tool from the University of Pennsylvania

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082.
  • A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082.
  • Sources indicate that but that remarkably high number doesn’t tell the full story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082. But that remarkably high number doesn’t tell the full story. Nearly half of Penn students receive financial aid, with 68% of those students having all of their tuition and fees covered by need-based assistance. But prospective students and their families often don’t know whether they’ll fall into that group, instead daunted by the university’s projected $100,000 price tag. The uncertainty around the cost of college contributes to Gen Z’s declining interest in four-year degree programs. As of 2026, just 37% of college graduates say they believe their degree was worth the cost, while less than half of high school students in the U.S. (44%) say they expect to earn a bachelor’s degree. The latter stat, from a 2022 survey, marked a 20-year low for college expectations. That’s why Penn has joined a growing cohort of universities offering cost calculators to students, using information like family size and income to project a student’s cost of attendance long before they’re ever admitted. Calculator culture To use Penn’s cost calculator, prospective students and their parents input data from their tax forms (or the forms themselves) as well as information like their marital status and the number of college students in their family currently enrolled. The calculator then returns a four-year estimate of the cost for that student to attend Penn, taking into account their projected need-based aid. While the calculator takes time to return a result, it also offers a selection of sample families to compare with. Are you closer to Hana, whose family makes $37,000 and has 86% of her tuition covered by Penn, or Nathan, whose family makes $425,000 and is paying the full tuition cost themselves? Another college offering a cost calculator is Brandeis University, which launched a tool called FAYE (an acronym for “financial aid you can expect”) in May. Brandeis also offers academic merit-based aid, so FAYE takes students’ transcripts into account along with financial and family data. Other colleges offer less-sophisticated estimates of students’ annual costs, not with calculators, but with graphs. Take Yale’s instant net price estimator, which shows a low, high, and best estimate of cost based on a family’s annual income. More than 60 other schools offer similar tools in collaboration with the College Board.

How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires. Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied. Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen. GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY The most important thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money, something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the organization went public in 2004. “Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.” Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment nearly 10 years later. “We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.” Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public. “If a company’s employees are coming to work just to make money, it’s over,” venture capitalist Paul Koontz said in 2004. “There need to be some bigger ambitions, some more fundamental calling that motivates a company.” GIVE WOULD-BE ENTREPRENEURS FREEDOM TO EXPERIMENT One of the biggest risks for post-IPO companies is that their most talented and entrepreneurial employees now have the resources to launch their own ventures. In fact, the effect is so powerful that at least one study has identified a causal link between the rate of IPOs in the economy and the rate of latest firm creation. While it may be impossible to prevent these exits altogether, post-IPO companies should ensure that their most talented staff have the freedom and resources to pursue their own ideas. “There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm said in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the company.” Management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe debuted a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required. “When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Mark Randall, formerly Adobe’s chief strategist and VP of creativity, told Fast Company. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.” DON’T LET WEALTH CREATE A NEW OFFICE HIERARCHY IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the company. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their net worth, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job. Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Stephen Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture. “The biggest mistake a company can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he said. Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.” PAY ATTENTION TO WELL-BEING AND WORKING CONDITIONS Employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions, knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away. And new stressors will emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. One study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined 10% and 6.6%, respectively, following IPOs. Post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Hollands-Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions. Management may also need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In a study published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996. They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees. “Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

In a recent development, typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

It has been revealed that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Industry observers note that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two important parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Sources indicate that swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a latest optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Industry observers note that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

In a recent development, this becomes particularly notable when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every notable API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document vital endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that below, Danny Meyer shares five key insights from his fresh book, What Could Possibly Go Right?
  • Meyer is a renowned restaurateur, entrepreneur, and founder of Union Square Hospitality Group and Shake Shack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that below, Danny Meyer shares five key insights from his newly introduced book, What Could Possibly Go Right? The Essential Journey to Scale an Enduring Culture. Meyer is a renowned restaurateur, entrepreneur, and founder of Union Square Hospitality Group and Shake Shack. He is widely recognized for his pioneering approach to hospitality and his belief that putting people first is the key to building great businesses. What’s the Substantial Idea? The best businesses do more than earn customers. They earn a place in people’s hearts by embracing change, refusing to settle for “good enough,” and making people’s lives genuinely better. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Meyer himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book. 1. What could possibly go right? I begin each day by asking myself this question because the really good stuff happens when I imagine the best possible outcome. Now, not everything goes right in life. But watch a really good card player and you’ll see that somehow they manage to win, even when they get the worst cards dealt to them. And that’s because even with a bad hand of cards, they start by saying, “Hmm, what would it take to actually make this work?” 2. Culture and growth are not in opposition. For many, many years, people would ask me, “How are you going to maintain your culture even with all the growth that you’re undertaking?” And I couldn’t answer them. Until finally, I had a wonderful “aha” moment: What if we could use our growth to advance our culture? Culture is like a shark. It cannot stay still. It doesn’t want to stay still. And in fact, it must be moving forward if it’s going to grow and survive. 3. Change your grip. I was the No. 5 player on my high school tennis team. I was pretty good, but never quite good enough to get to No. 4, No. 3, and certainly not No. 2 or 1. But my coach gave me an important piece of advice. He mentioned, “Look, you’re good enough right now. You’ve made the team, but if you really want to excel and improve your game, you’re going to have to change your grip.” And so he turned the tennis racket maybe a quarter of an inch in my hand. My hold on the racket felt so awkward. The next five balls I hit sailed over the fence. The next five after that went right into the net. He said, “Look, stick with this thing and you’ll get more velocity. You’ll get more top spin.” But I chose to revert. In business, I’ve learned to constantly be changing my grip. Whatever got me here is not going to get me there, and though it’s uncomfortable to make those changes, it’s a key to outstanding leadership. 4. Don’t effing settle (DFS). Great companies rarely collapse overnight. Instead, they decline slowly through small compromises, lowered standards, or tolerated misses. Soon, average begins to feel normal and normal is not essential. In my firm culture, we bring the DFS model to everything from the hiring process to daily routines. We ask, “Is it good enough? Is the person a good enough hire? Is the way we’re doing things good enough to take us to the next level?” A DFS mentality reminds everyone in the organization that there is nothing positive about settling in terms of getting us to the next level. As a matter of fact, complacency—doing things in an average way—is the worst possible thing you can do for the culture of your business because you’re going to stop attracting the best performers, and then your best performers are going to start to feel demoralized because you’ve surrounded them with sub-performers. 5. Essentiality. My goal is to create businesses that become essential in people’s lives. I’d like every single thing we do to make people’s lives better to the point that they think, My life improved because that place existed. And, God forbid, if the place went out of business, people would actually feel a sense of sadness or diminishment. Think about the handful of songs in your life that always make you feel good every single time you hear them. The songs that make you think, “I can’t even imagine my life if that song had never been written.” That’s what we want to do with restaurants. It is amazing when any company does that with any product. Think about the way nonessential things weigh down our lives. You can turn on Netflix and there are way more movies and way more TV series than you can possibly consume in a lifetime. Wouldn’t you love it if you could just curate the ones that were actually essential? That’s what we try to do when we create a business, and I think that is a worthy goal. Before the internet, the No. 1 thing we tried to earn as a business was mindshare. We wanted people to know we existed. But then, our game became: How can we earn heartshare? How can we earn a place in people’s hearts so that they fall in love with what we do? If you earn heartshare over and over, that is the pathway to essentiality. Global OLED monitor shipments doubled year-over-year in Q3 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce.
  • Sources indicate that ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments.
  • Recent findings suggest that price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce. Shipments also increased 13% sequentially, reflecting strong demand for OLED displays and improving panel availability. While the market's rapid growth is impressive regardless, there are good reasons why OLED monitors are becoming increasingly popular: they're getting cheaper, better, and considerably easier to justify.

Sources indicate that ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments. MSI climbed into second place for the first time, capturing 14.5% of the market, while Samsung slipped to third with 11.3%. Both Taiwanese vendors have been particularly aggressive in the gaming monitor market, where increasingly competitive pricing has helped make OLED technology accessible to more buyers, while ubiquitous advertising with tech-conscious gamers has made them highly visible. According to Omdia, mainstream 27-inch QHD 240Hz OLED gaming monitors have seen price cuts exceeding 40% in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though. Earlier generations of OLED monitors had some fairly significant compromises, particularly their relatively limited brightness and unconventional subpixel arrangements that could cause colored fringing around text. Newer tandem OLED panels offer improved brightness and color reproduction, while RGB-stripe OLED layouts bring much cleaner text rendering. These improvements are making OLEDs considerably more attractive as everyday desktop monitors, rather than merely excellent gaming displays with major caveats.

Industry observers note that there's also an interesting macroeconomic angle to OLED's growth. The AI industry's insatiable appetite for memory and storage has made upgrading a gaming PC considerably more expensive. DRAM component prices have increased severalfold, while NAND flash and hard drive availability have also been squeezed by demand from AI data centers—though there are early signs of some relief, at least on the flash memory front. Graphics cards, especially (but not exclusively) at the high end, are increasingly difficult to find at anything resembling reasonable prices.

Sources indicate that monitors, meanwhile, aren't directly subject to the same supply pressures affecting DRAM, NAND, and discrete GPUs. That makes upgrading a display an appealing alternative for gamers who aren't particularly interested in spending a small fortune on an entirely newly introduced PC. An OLED monitor can substantially improve the gaming experience without requiring a new graphics card, memory kit, or storage drive. The contrast, response times, and color gamut of OLEDs far outstrip even the best LCDs, and that's to say nothing of their superior HDR reproduction thanks to the inherent self-emissive nature of OLED panels.

With OLED prices falling and the technology's longstanding limitations becoming less noticeable, a fresh monitor is becoming one of the more compelling upgrades available to PC gamers. Indeed, several of our picks for the best gaming monitors, including the best overall, best 4K, and best ultrawide, are based on OLED technology. Though concerns about burn-in and limited lifespan remain, there's no question that OLED is the best display technology we have right now.

#11484. Tech Report: You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (403 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.
  • Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication.
  • You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.

Industry observers note that text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a new one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

…you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your prepares change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.).

In a recent development, email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”.

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

According to recent reports, you can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this upcoming Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when announced in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”.

#11483. The legal standard that could help rein in AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2008 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

The legal standard that could help rein in AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating.
  • In a recent development, some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating.
  • In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that its ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting. In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that its ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide. The state of Kentucky later filed suit, claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation. Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused. Regulating AI was a hot concern during the 2026 midterms, too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda. I am a former litigator and a professor of business law, and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm. But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability. Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants. Abnormally dangerous software Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store. Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent, or had no intent to create trouble. A 2026 lawsuit claims ChatGPT encouraged a young woman to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity, such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it. AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “the utmost care to prevent the harm.” An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox—a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network—but loses control of it. The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose. One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage. Lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn’t available to most people. Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately. In 1929, aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous. But damages were capped at $8,300, which was not a large deterrent. Attitudes changed in 1999, when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide. It raised statutory damages and eliminated caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company’s aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes. Guilty products Strict product liability is the other strategy for holding AI companies responsible for harm. In years past, courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible. But that view is shifting. In recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable. Cases against Facebook have fallen into this category. Character.AI’s recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. “Design defects” is the part of the doctrine gaining traction. To use this, a plaintiff highlights that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it. So far, the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots. Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags. A court might order that AI software be turned off, or “grounded,” until it is improved. But as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone’s daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use. Moving target AI software by its nature is constantly “learning” and therefore changing. It is impossible for a company to promise that AI software will absolutely behave a certain way. In many cases, AI software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible, “even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers,” according to a Brookings Institution report. I believe that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues. The next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product, and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated. Deven Desai is a professor of business law and ethics and an associate director for law, policy, and ethics at the Machine Learning Center at the Georgia Institute of Technology. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small enhancement to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small enhancement to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

In a recent development, like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

It has been revealed that this joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now swiftly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.
