#11480. The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2538 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware firm with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise.
  • He planned and founded the company in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area.
  • All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware firm with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise.

He planned and founded the company in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area. After more than 30 years, Nvidia had thousands of employees, a global footprint, and a name that people equated to AI chips.

All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation. Let’s go back and see how it all began. This is an ongoing saga, so we have listed stories related to the scandal below, which we will enhancement as events unfold.

Jensen resigned from Nvidia on November 12, after two weeks of news reports accusing him of multiple affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with his own subordinate. This is significant for Nvidia, which has had a single CEO since its inception. Huang was the face of the tech giant, and many of its employees, shareholders, partners, and fans still support him despite the circumstances of his departure. He steered Nvidia into the giant that it is today by having the vision to develop CUDA nearly 20 years before ChatGPT made AI accessible to the average user and buying companies that helped it scale deployments to hundreds of thousands of AI GPUs.

By 2022, ChatGPT’s arrival and subsequent boom set the AI race in motion, with tech giants and AI startups buying up as many GPUs as they could get their hands on. The increased demand for Nvidia’s products caused it to break the trillion-dollar mark in less than a year after the release of OpenAI’s LLM. As the largest individual shareholders of the manufacturer, Huang and his wife, Lori, became some of the wealthiest people in the world.

In a recent development, the billionaire founder hasn't always gloated about his position. He once said in a podcast that if he could turn back time, he wouldn’t have founded Nvidia at all, and also cringed at the praises that the Caltech Board of Trustees chairperson heaped on him before he gave the 2024 keynote speech at the institute’s commencement exercises. He has frequently cited his history working as a “Dishwasher, Busboy, Waiter” at Denny’s, noting it under his experience on his LinkedIn page. More than that, people have seen Jensen go where other celebrity CEOs are rarely seen — enjoying street food in Vietnam, dining at a local fried chicken joint in Korea, and even dragging along 35 of Taiwan’s semiconductor CEOs to a restaurant in Taipei.

Sources indicate that but even as he’s building his “Man of the People” persona, his position as the head of arguably the most vital chipmaker in the AI industry meant that he was also gaining influence in business and governance. Industry leaders noticed the power that Nvidia held over those who want GPUs to train their AI models, with some of his fellow billionaires begging him over dinner to sell them GPUs. Just weeks into President Donald Trump’s second term, Jensen Huang was meeting with him at the White House, discussing AI policy and hardware export controls — something the Biden administration started in 2022 in an attempt to hold back China’s ambition'sin AI.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that the rivalry between the U.S. and China has been simmering for years, with Chinese companies like Huawei getting blacklisted because of their work with the People’s Liberation Army. In August 2022, about three months before ChatGPT made AI a household term, Washington expanded its trade bans on Beijing and imposed export controls on Nvidia’s H100 and A100 GPUs. The company responded to this by building a new data center GPU that conformed to U.S. standards specifically for the Chinese market, called the A800, by November of that year. Despite delivering only 70% of the performance of the A100 it was based on, the GPU reportedly still saw great demand from Chinese customers.

It has been revealed that however, the A800 only had a relatively short run as the Biden administration once again increased the performance threshold in October 2023, which resulted in the export prohibition of A800 and H800 GPUs to China. This move forced the tech giant to iterate once again, creating new models that it could sell to Chinese companies, like the Nvidia H20. These chips arrived on the market in early 2024, but before the Biden administration ended in January 2025, it proposed even stricter rules called the AI Diffusion Policy. This sorted nations into different tiers based on trust and risk levels — countries in tier 1, which includes the U.S. and its closest allies, have minimal restrictions, while those in tier 3 are effectively barred from receiving advanced AI GPUs containing U.S. technology.

In a recent development, this is problematic for Nvidia, as China is the second-largest computer market in the world t and represented between 20% and 25% of Nvidia's data center sales. The company lobbied the U.S. government to ease AI GPU export restrictions, with Trump reportedly suspending the proposed Nvidia H20 ban after Jensen spent $1 million to have dinner with the president in early April 2025. The White House went ahead anyway and banned the sale of the AI GPU less than a week after that, resulting in a $5.5 billion write-off for the company.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang himself had harsh comments about Washington’s trade ban, saying that “export control was a failure,” and that it had caused the firm’s AI GPU market share in China to go from 95% to zero. He even argued that “conceding an entire market the size of China probably does not make a lot of strategic sense, so I think that has already largely backfired.”.

Sources indicate that but even as Huang was fighting to have the trade ban on the Nvidia H20 chip lifted, he continued praising Trump’s tariff strategy, calling it “utterly visionary.” The president eventually reversed the ban three months later, and by December 2025, he had approved Nvidia H200 exports to China, but only if Nvidia pays a 25% fee. The newer Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips remain out of reach for Chinese companies, though — at least on paper.

Allegations that Chinese companies have been breaking Washington’s trade ban and smuggling Nvidia AI GPUs into China have been circulating since June 2023, after Reuters revealed that vendors in Shenzhen could secure A100 chips when asked discreetly. They reportedly bought these chips from the excess stocks sold in the open market or through intermediaries in India, Taiwan, and Singapore. Another story published in January 2024 asserted that the Chinese military and related institutions, state-run data centers, and even universities continue buying banned A100 and H100 chips. Six months after that, accounts of underground networks dedicated to smuggling AI GPUs — even entire servers — through other countries started emerging.

In 2025, an investigative report revealed that at least a billion dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI chips were allegedly funneled into China. Some sellers likened the illicit AI GPU trade to a seafood market, with brokers and retailers openly advertising the most advanced Nvidia AI chips online, from RTX 5090 GPUs to complete B200 servers.

Sources indicate that even with all these reports, Huang continued denying that Nvidia’s chips were being smuggled into China. “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion,” the then-CEO told reporters at Computex 2025. He also added, “The Grace Blackwell system is nearly two tons, and so you’re not going to be shipping — you’re not going to be putting that in your pocket or your backpack anytime soon. And so, these systems are fairly easy to keep track of... but the key thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed, and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology, and so they very well monitor themselves very carefully and they’re quite careful about that.”.

Industry observers note that in the midst of all these AI chip smuggling rumors, the Bureau of Industry and Security, the agency in charge of enforcing U.S. trade sanctions, was found to be “inadequate” and underfunded, and it has been relying on outdated manual processes to enforce restrictions on Chinese tech companies. Despite that, companies and individuals across the world are being investigated and arrested for bypassing Washington’s export controls.

Singaporean authorities broke up a smuggling ring in early 2025 that smuggled Nvidia GPUs for Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, resulting in a raid of 22 different locations and the arrest of nine people. In October of the same year, a Singapore company called Megaspeed, which was led by Alice Huang, allegedly diverted $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Four Americans were then arrested the following month for shipping 400 Nvidia A100s and attempting to send 50 more Nvidia H200 GPUs to China.

It has been revealed that an even bigger smuggling scandal unfolded some four months after the arrests, after three Super Micro employees were arrested for smuggling $2.5 billion of Nvidia hardware into China. The suspects included company co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, although Super Micro itself was not implicated. The Super Micro case spanned the globe, with Taiwanese authorities raiding 12 locations related to the case in May 2026, with another nine sites and six people investigated in June. Jensen Huang urged the company to fix its export control compliance after the arrests and raids, telling the media, “We insist our partners are compliant. We hope that they will enhance and improve their regulatory compliance and prevent that from happening in the future.”.

But just five months after he made this statement, one stunning accusation unraveled it all.

Recent findings suggest that on October 29, 2026, The New York Times published a report that Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot through the executive of a firm who was “close” to him — that executive is Alice Huang. Nvidia denied the accusation. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” a company spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.".

In a recent development, but a little over a week later, U.S. intelligence sources claimed that the former Nvidia chief had an affair with the Megaspeed executive. This is the same Megaspeed that has been accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to the tune of $2 billion. By the evening of Sunday, November 8, Jensen admitted to the affair, although he did not name the third party in his statement.

Recent findings suggest that many government officials would usually turn a blind eye towards a tech executive’s personal life, but the fact that he is the leader of the U.S.’s premier AI chip maker and that he is also close to the president has caught the attention of authorities. This has led to the U.S. Congress asking him to a closed-door meeting to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and the FBI investigating his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy.

The admission and allegations led to people digging deeper into Alice Huang. An investigation by The Information revealed that she was connected to a “labyrinth” of companies spanning Singapore, China, and the British Virgin Islands, and that she allegedly helped move around $7.5 billion worth of AI GPU imports. $2 billion was routed from Megaspeed to Speedmatrix, its Malaysia subsidiary, while another $4.6 billion moved directly from the Singaporean manufacturer into Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based cloud services company. It has also reportedly bought Nvidia GPUs from other sources, resulting in the estimated total value of its imports.

People close to her also stated that she would leverage her relationship with Jensen to customers, often posting pictures with him on her WeChat account, showing potential clients unpublished photos with the Nvidia chief, and even boasting that he would take her to dinner and give her gifts on her birthday. It also seems that Alice Huang was not acting alone. Multiple sources say that Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband, was central to the operation to acquire AI GPUs. He even seemingly acknowledged her relationship with Jensen Huang and has jokingly said that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire.

However, it seems that the straw that broke the camel’s back was another allegation that Jensen had an affair with another woman — this time, with Kimberly Powell, the firm’s vice president of health care who directly reported to him. Hours after this revelation, the company board revealed that Jensen had resigned from all his leadership positions at Nvidia, with employees saying he looked “broken and shattered” as he left the company he spent over three decades building in disgrace. Nvidia is looking for internal and external CEO candidates. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive.

In a recent development, it may be the end of an era, but this does not necessarily spell the end for Jensen Huang. Despite his sudden downfall and quick removal from Nvidia, his status as the king of AI infrastructure remains valuable to the AI industry. Elon Musk even mentioned on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him, and this could ring true for any business that wants to break into the semiconductor space. But does he even want to return?Huang's first public statement after his resignation came on X on Nov. 17, in which the former CEO said he has "outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," and that if asked by the firm's board, he would be "honored" to take the job.".

It has been revealed that over 190,000 shareholders, partners, current and former employees, and fans, including Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, have signed an online petition to bring him back as the leader of the company. President Donald Trump called for his reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.The board, however, may not see things the same way. Multiple reports suggest that the board isn't considering bringing Huang back, and instead is focusing on a latest candidate, the ongoing investigation into Huang, and preparing for national security investigations.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The K-shaped economy strikes again—and this time it’s impacting the country’s ailing Social Security system.
  • As you may have heard, Social Security’s trustees have estimated that unless the federal government acts soon, the retirement trust fund will become insolvent as early as the fourth quarter of 2032, in about six years, while the combined trust fund will run out in 2034—leaving Social Security able to fund only about 80% of promised benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the K-shaped economy strikes again—and this time it’s impacting the country’s ailing Social Security system. As you may have heard, Social Security’s trustees have estimated that unless the federal government acts soon, the retirement trust fund will become insolvent as early as the fourth quarter of 2032, in about six years, while the combined trust fund will run out in 2034—leaving Social Security able to fund only about 80% of promised benefits. The benefit cuts would affect tens of millions of Americans. Some 71 million—54 million retired workers and 9 million of their survivors and dependents—currently receive Social Security benefits. But what you may not know is the reason for the potential shortfall: Up until now, many critics and politicians have primarily blamed the program’s insolvency on the country’s growing older population, and mismanagement of the trust. (Republican Senator Ron Johnson from Wisconsin even called it “an illegal Ponzi scheme.”) But in a latest report, the AARP argues there is another main driver: changing income patterns, and the growing wealth inequality in the U.S. that’s eating into Social Security’s revenue base, which is primarily financed through payroll taxes applied to earnings up to a statutory cap. According to the report, those shifting income patterns have shortened the Social Security trust fund’s lifespan by 25 years. “Over time, a declining share of the nation’s gross domestic product has been subject to this [payroll] tax, as earnings above the cap have grown rapidly, driven by rising wages among high-income workers, whereas earnings below the cap have increased more slowly,” the AARP report claims. In 2027, earnings over $192,300 won’t be taxed for Social Security at all. “It implies the wealthiest Americans aren’t paying their fair share,” Robert Laura, a financial planner and founder of the Retirement Coaches Association, told Fast Firm. In a K-shaped economy, the gap between the richest and poorest widens, as high-income individuals continue to prosper while lower-income consumers increasingly struggle. As the AARP argues, that means less money is going toward funding Social Security, adding pressure on the trust’s finances. Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has been trying to rally his colleagues to come up with a way to avoid a Social Security crisis when the 120th Congress convenes in January. Sanders recently reiterated his strategy, known as the “Bernie bump,” that would raise benefits “by at least $2,400 a year and extend Social Security’s solvency for generations.” If Sanders’s previous Social Security Expansion Act proposal passed, it would extend benefits beyond the current annual cost-of-living adjustments, which are meant to keep pace with inflation, and will increase payments 3.6% in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after a no-good, very bad week for AI stocks, SpaceX gave the AI faithful—and all the Elon Musk acolytes—something to celebrate when it reported earnings on October 20.
  • After a no-good, very bad week for AI stocks, SpaceX gave the AI faithful—and all the Elon Musk acolytes—something to celebrate when it reported earnings on October 20.
  • Industry observers note that since I’m a curmudgeon and since you can read about what there is to like in a lot of other places, I’ll tell you what is not to like!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after a no-good, very bad week for AI stocks, SpaceX gave the AI faithful—and all the Elon Musk acolytes—something to celebrate when it reported earnings on October 20. Its results beat analyst expectations across the board in almost every way, with revenue leaping 161% to $14.6 billion, and operating income hitting $2.8 billion. Even its so-called Super Intelligence segment—its AI business—reported $431 million in operating income, a welcome relief from the red ink that is a chief worry about AI companies. The stock surged 8%, JPMorgan doubled its price target to $500 a share, and Truist Securities called the results “the first data point during earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers.” What’s not to like? Since I’m a curmudgeon and since you can read about what there is to like in a lot of other places, I’ll tell you what is not to like! But first, let me offer a trigger warning for those who can’t bear to hear anything bad about Elon Musk. Second, a caveat: This is meant to provide those who want to test their optimism a few counterpoints, not to reflect my complete views on the company. To start with the obvious, SpaceX is priced less like an actual company than like a precious object that should be in a museum. It is now valued at $2.1 trillion, which is about 36 times its annualized revenue and roughly 55 times its annualized adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization). That’s a premium that only a few other companies, like Palantir and Cloudflare, command. And as a source points out to me, that $2.1 trillion is almost twice the $1.28 trillion combined market value of the seven biggest defense giants—Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics, and so on. These are real companies, upon which the American economy depends. Does SpaceX’s premium reflect economic reality? The profitability of both SpaceX overall and of the AI segment also merits a second look. The company’s accounting profit didn’t translate into free cash flow. Indeed, free cash flow burn was almost $10 billion, exceeding the expectations of a burn of $8.6 billion. In the AI business alone, SpaceX spent $16.4 billion in the quarter. There’s nothing wrong with spending cash in the expectation that the investments will turn into profits someday. But it does mean the company is dependent on the capital markets to supply the funding it needs to grow. The larger matter is that SpaceX has effectively turned its AI business into a neocloud. Its own model, xAI, is badly lagging others, based on the reported token spend per model. XAI’s spend is a fraction of that of market leaders Anthropic and OpenAI. Whether because xAI was failing or because he spotted an opportunity, Musk pivoted to selling computing power to other players. That means that some of the same factors that affect a company like CoreWeave, which saw its stock plummet and the yield on its bonds soar last month because of its heavy cash burn and constant need to raise capital, also affect SpaceX’s AI business. On the earnings call, Musk told analysts to expect 10 gigawatts of incremental compute to come online during 2027. According to a back-of-the-envelope calculation done by longtime skeptic Jim Chanos, for the most cutting-edge fully equipped data centers, that would require $500 billion-plus of capital expenditures, which is three times higher than the consensus view of what the entire company will spend in 2027. On the call, SpaceX management claimed they have debt lined up to finance the CapEx spree. “There are a number of available pools of debt capital that we are talking to at the moment relating to funding this incredible growth,” said CFO Brad Coffman. But it’s increasingly unclear if bond markets will absorb the sheer amount of debt all the AI companies proposal to issue without charging higher rates—and, of course, higher rates make profitability more elusive. Like other neoclouds, SpaceX also depends to some degree on customers that are themselves losing money. In the past quarter, SpaceX confirmed contracts with Anthropic, Google, and the startup Reflection AI, another AI model company. Google is obviously a rock-solid company. But Reflection AI loses money, as does Anthropic. With Anthropic’s IPO, the company will have a lot of cash with which to continue to pay suppliers like SpaceX. But someday, SpaceX’s customers have to be able to generate their own profits. Until that happens, even if SpaceX itself is producing profits, the capital markets still have to be willing to fund its customers, or SpaceX’s business goes away, too. In the short term, that could eventually pose a problem. “There does not appear to be a single enterprise customer for AI who pays the vendor more than it costs to deliver the service,” notes longtime investor Roger McNamee. In the most recent quarter, SpaceX’s revenue per megawatt of compute delivered—a common industry shorthand for measuring data center economics—soared from $8.5 million per megawatt in the second quarter to $19.5 million per average megawatt in this quarter, according to Chanos’s calculation. That number is better than the roughly $11 per megawatt that he says the average neocloud reports. But it’s below the $40 million to $50 million per megawatt that bulls argued last summer compute would fetch. Which gets to the biggest issue. SpaceX is making a huge bet that the price of compute will continue to climb. Musk said that the company prefers to sell short-term contracts priced at the spot market, because he expects the price to keep rising. He isn’t hedging the risk that it will instead fall by locking in lots of long-term contracts. That’s probably why SpaceX’s revenue per megawatt is higher than other neoclouds’. “It is not impossible that we will have a six-month payback period for compute next year,” Musk said on the call. But parsing the numbers demonstrates just what kind of premium pricing Musk is counting on. SpaceX says it is on track for $100 billion in annualized recurring revenue in its AI business by year-end 2026, and is forecasting $500 billion to $1 trillion in AI annual recurring revenue by year-end 2027. If Chanos is right that the additional 10 gigawatts of compute capacity will require about $500 billion in capital expenditures, then SpaceX will have to produce between $1 and $2 of revenue for every dollar of capital expenditures. He estimates that presently, the AI industry is producing only about 30 cents of annual revenue for every dollar of infrastructure spending, so SpaceX is planning to get between three and seven times the industry’s current ratio. There is certainly an argument that compute prices will only continue to rise, and that by positioning itself to take maximum advantage of the increases, SpaceX is making a smart bet. “The use cases are accelerating and we see it in the field every day, and the CapEx dollars will be in the trillions with a massive ripple impact across the economy,” writes one bull, Dan Ives of Yorkville. But welcome to the great AI debate, in which for every bull there is a bear. So, of course, there’s also an argument that compute prices won’t rise. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the AI business is not all systems go. “Corporate America has been very uneven in its ability to extract value from its AI models,” Citadel CEO Ken Griffin said at Citadel’s Future of Global Markets conference in Fresh York City. “I think all of corporate America is looking at their bills from Anthropic and OpenAI and going: ‘OK, we need to think about how to make sure we’re getting productivity out of this.’” Axios also recently reported that prices for tokens—a measure of AI usage—are plummeting. It’s possible that might stimulate more demand. But if corporate America does pull back on its spending on AI—if companies aren’t finding AI useful enough to continue to ramp up the spend—it’s hard to see how that doesn’t affect compute prices at some point. Apart from the AI business, SpaceX also has its traditional space business, which is basically break-even, and Starlink. Starlink is a good, if not great, business—one that generated $2.4 billion of operating profit in the quarter. But combined, they are nowhere near enough to support a $2.1 trillion valuation. Before the IPO, Morningstar analyst Nicolas Owens argued that if investors were just getting the rockets and Starlink and AI didn’t work out, SpaceX could be worth as little as $40 a share. SpaceX may well confound the skeptics, including me, as Musk has done so many times before. His companies have accomplished things people said were impossible. But it’s also worth remembering that not everything Musk says will happen does happen, at least not on the schedule he predicts, be it solar roofs, full self-driving cars, or Optimus robots. And at some point—who knows when, but there will be a point—the company will have to show that it is on a clear path to generate enough cash to validate the extraordinary prices that investors are paying. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • In a recent development, AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Industry observers note that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

In a recent development, softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real consumers can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free initiative is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app customers, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

According to recent reports, lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every initiative, Free included.

Sources indicate that base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Sources indicate that replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Industry observers note that glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Industry observers note that bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Recent findings suggest that bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Recent findings suggest that retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

Industry observers note that v0's Free initiative gives new owners $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Sources indicate that figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Sources indicate that three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

In a recent development, building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

Industry observers note that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chemical spill at a SpaceXAI facility in Southaven saw the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) get involved, with between 5,000 and 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol confirmed to have spilled. The chemical is a heat transfer fluid used in a variety of products, such as antifreeze. The chemical ultimately found its way into a drainage ditch, but MDEQ has told residents that there is no immediate threat to their health or safety, according to local news reports.

Industry observers note that however, it has also been confirmed that water samples will be collected for further laboratory analysis while workers continue to clean the area and monitor for any further issues. It's also been reported that the chemical was contained to the drainage ditch and did not reach the nearby Horn Lake Creek.

In a recent development, it hasn't been a great November for SpaceXAI in Southaven. Earlier this month, it suffered a setback in a lawsuit over pollution in the area caused by its data center. The April 2026 suit targets the company's gas-powered power plant, which is used to supply power for its facility in the Greater Memphis area. It's argued that 27 gas turbines were installed without obtaining the required permits. It's also alleged that the plant could emit more than 5,000 tons of nitrogen oxides and 47 tons of formaldehyde — a cancer-causing chemical — annually. The company has tried to classify the turbines as mobile units to get around the issue, but a judge rejected that manoeuvre.

In a recent development, clearly aware of the local sentiment towards its presence, SpaceXAI offered a 50% Starlink discount to anyone living near its two Memphis data centers. SpaceXAI said that, between late June and early September, around 2,000 residents of the greater Memphis and Southaven area had signed up for Starlink connectivity.

It was also recently announced that the City of Memphis was ready to make its first major investment as part of its new Community Benefits Ordinance, a fund that uses revenue from SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 facility. Tech Report: Nvidia indicates it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials.
  • “There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right?
  • Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26, calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd.".

“There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder said. “But what we do have as a manufacturer, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.”.

Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder claims the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?”.

Although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, reveals up in two places. Grace, Finder notes, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core.

The picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents.

This “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.”.

Recent findings suggest that although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.”.

It has been revealed that as you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking, the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking, the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available.

Sources indicate that A portion of the AI industry is focused on tackling the problem of fully utilizing the GPU, Nvidia included. GPUs shouldn’t sit idle for very long (if at all) with the demand today, and they don’t. The challenge today is spinning up these agent sandboxes quickly, within milliseconds, so that the CPU isn’t sitting idle, either.

Finder provided an example of using a coding agent. If you’ve used a coding agent before, you’re probably familiar with this process. After prompting, the model will make several small tool calls to read and locate files, passing back to the model in between. These are tiny calls, almost negligible, and the vast majority of the time is spent in the model on the GPU. Then, it may start compiling and testing the project, which is much more bound by the CPU. The GPU, Finder says, isn't sitting idle during that time. It’s being leveraged for another purpose. Finder suggests “that very same thing is going to happen on the CPU.”.

Sources indicate that this “very interesting computer science problem,” as Finder described it, is being investigated by AI startups such as Daytona and E2B to spin up and close down agentic sandboxes in milliseconds. And serving more agents will naturally put pressure on the memory system, which is an area where Vera has an edge. “We built a product that does really, really well without such optimizations, but as a design point that really will lean into them when the industry starts to catch up to this,” Finder noted.

Industry observers note that vera is a fascinating chip, regardless of what you think of it and how it’s presented in marketing materials (from Nvidia itself or elsewhere). Although Grace was the starting point internally, Vera has ridden the wave of agentic to become a much bigger player in the world of CPUs, and Nvidia has already announced that it will follow up with its Rosa CPU featuring the new Rigel microarchitecture. Vera is an opinionated CPU indeed, and time will tell if that opinion is correct.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

In a recent development, “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta upgrade, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

Recent findings suggest that this guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

Industry observers note that • Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

Recent findings suggest that • Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

Sources indicate that cudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it claims it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your strategy. It indicates to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

Recent findings suggest that GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

It has been revealed that strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and states other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Sources indicate that copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it states it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Industry observers note that limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

According to recent reports, originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, states very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

According to recent reports, strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

In a recent development, sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page states false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Industry observers note that • False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

Industry observers note that • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

According to recent reports, • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

Industry observers note that openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

In a recent development, most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

Industry observers note that • Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

Industry observers note that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and patch as newly introduced models appear.

Industry observers note that • Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

According to recent reports, because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

In a recent development, • Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

Recent findings suggest that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

Industry observers note that • Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

Sources indicate that • Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

According to recent reports, they can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Recent findings suggest that yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

It has been revealed that sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

In a recent development, AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

#11462. Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (512 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, while Ohioans have rejected the building of new data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future.
  • Legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power company, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one.
  • Industry observers note that this follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for newly introduced transmission lines needed to power new data centers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while Ohioans have rejected the building of new data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future. That's if a newly leaked bill that could allow data centers to be classified as public utilities is allowed to progress. The move would see the list of who can qualify for eminent domain law expanded, moving beyond entities owned or operated by municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The bill, leaked to WCPO Cincinnati, would add "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities.".

Legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power company, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one. The writing has been on the wall for a while, too, after it was discovered in June that the Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law to "extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.”.

Industry observers note that this follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for newly introduced transmission lines needed to power new data centers. The law gives the government the power to take private land without the need for the owner's consent, so long as it is for public use and the owner receives appropriate compensation. The government can also delegate the same land-grabbing power to “private entities or common carriers,” which includes utility companies.

Sources indicate that this is already happening, too. Earlier this year, the largest utility firm in Georgia required the removal of 30 residential properties in order to upgrade its grid. Residents claimed that the expansion was to power AI data centers, a fact given more weight by the fact that one such data center was located just a few miles away.

Despite this, eminent domain law can still be used for good. Nashville set out to use the same law to block the building of a 69,220-square-foot single-story data center next to a zoo. Nashville Metro Council approved the use of eminent domain as a way to buy the land from a local developer who planned the $700 million data center buildout.
